facts.claim: Eagle landed on the Moon on 20 July 1969
facts.evidence: The LM landed at 20:17:40 UT (4:17:40 p.m. EDT) on 20 July 1969

facts.claim: Landing coordinates (from LRO images)
facts.evidence: 0.67416 degrees N latitude, 23.47314 degrees E longitude (as determined from Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter images

facts.claim: First crewed vehicle to land on the Moon
facts.evidence: was the first crewed vehicle to land on the Moon

facts.claim: Crew on the surface: Neil A. Armstrong and Edwin E. "Buzz" Aldrin Jr.
facts.evidence: It carried two astronauts, Commander Neil A. Armstrong and LM pilot Edwin E.

facts.claim: Descent engine burn to the surface
facts.evidence: At 20:05 the LM descent engine fired for 756.3 seconds

facts.claim: Armstrong stepped onto the surface
facts.evidence: Armstrong stepped onto the lunar surface at 02:56:15 UT on 21 July

facts.claim: Aldrin followed 19 minutes later
facts.evidence: Aldrin followed 19 minutes later

facts.claim: Crew unveiled the plaque on a strut behind the ladder and read it aloud
facts.evidence: unveiled the plaque mounted on a strut behind the ladder and read the inscription aloud

facts.claim: Plaque inscription as transcribed by NSSDCA (the engraving itself, visible in AS11-40-5899, reads "upon the Moon"; the website quotes the engraving)
facts.value: Here men from the planet Earth first set foot on the Moon July 1969, A.D. We came in peace for all mankind.
facts.evidence: Here men from the planet Earth first set foot on the Moon July 1969, A.D. We came in peace for all mankind.

facts.claim: Plaque fixed to the ladder on the landing-gear strut, covered by steel sheet in flight
facts.evidence: The plaque was attached to the ladder on the landing gear strut on the descent stage

facts.claim: Plaque size (stainless steel)
facts.value: 9 x 7 5/8 in, 1/16 in thick (about 23 x 19 cm)
facts.evidence: measuring nine by seven and five-eighths inches, and one-sixteenth inch thick

facts.claim: Ascent stage lifted off after 21 h 36 min on the surface
facts.evidence: The LM lifted off from the Moon at 17:54:01 UT on 21 July after 21 hours, 36 minutes on the lunar surface.

facts.claim: Fate of the ascent stage unknown; assumed to have crashed within 1 to 4 months
facts.evidence: The fate of the LM is not known, but it is assumed that it crashed into the lunar surface sometime within the following 1 to 4 months.

facts.claim: The descent stage served as launch platform and was left on the Moon
facts.evidence: The descent stage served as a platform for launching the ascent stage and was left behind on the Moon.

facts.claim: Descent stage shape and size
facts.value: octagonal prism 4.2 m across, 1.7 m thick
facts.evidence: octagonal prism 4.2 meters across and 1.7 m thick

facts.claim: Legs held the stage bottom 1.5 m above the surface
facts.evidence: held the bottom of the stage 1.5 m above the surface

facts.claim: Distance between opposite footpads
facts.evidence: The distance between the ends of the footpads on opposite landing legs was 9.4 m.

facts.claim: One leg had an egress platform (porch) and ladder
facts.evidence: One of the legs had a small astronaut egress platform and ladder.

facts.claim: Descent engine skirt about 1 m long
facts.evidence: A one meter long conical descent engine skirt protruded from the bottom of the stage.

facts.claim: Tanks carried in the descent stage
facts.value: Aerozine 50, nitrogen tetroxide, water, oxygen, helium
facts.evidence: two tanks of aerozine 50 fuel, two tanks of nitrogen tetroxide oxidizer, water, oxygen and helium tanks

facts.claim: Descent engine maximum thrust (deep-throttling)
facts.evidence: deep-throttling ablative rocket with a maximum thrust of about 45,000 N

facts.claim: Descent stage dry mass and initial propellant
facts.evidence: The descent stage dry mass (including stowed surface equipment) was 2034 kg and 8248 kg of propellant were onboard initially.

facts.claim: On Apollo 15, 16 and 17 the descent stage also carried the lunar rover
facts.evidence: in the case of Apollo 15, 16, and 17, the lunar rover

facts.claim: The experiments package was stowed in the descent stage scientific equipment bay
facts.evidence: scientific equipment bay

facts.claim: Lunar samples collected
facts.evidence: collected 21.55 kg of lunar rock and soil

facts.claim: Samples (MSFC caption figure)
facts.evidence: collected 47 pounds of lunar surface material

facts.claim: Experiments package (EASEP) site about 17 m south of the LM
facts.evidence: The EASEP was deployed approximately 17 m south of the LM, at 0.6735 N latitude, 23.4730 E longitude

facts.claim: Reflector deployed about 5 m north-northwest of the EASEP; needs no power
facts.evidence: It was deployed about 5 meters NNW of the EASEP.

facts.claim: Reflector required no power
facts.evidence: required no power

facts.claim: Built of fused-silica cubes on a folding support aimed at Earth
facts.evidence: folding support structure for aiming and aligning the array toward earth. The array was built of cubes of fused silica.

facts.claim: Principal investigator
facts.value: Carroll O. Alley, University of Maryland
facts.evidence: Carroll O. Alley

facts.claim: Apollo 11 and 14 arrays: 100 corner cubes each; Apollo 15: 300
facts.evidence: The Apollo 11 and 14 arrays have 100 quartz glass prisms (called corner cubes) each, while the array of Apollo 15 has 300.

facts.claim: The arrays require no power
facts.evidence: The arrays themselves require no power.

facts.claim: Observatories using the arrays (as of NASA 2019 article)
facts.evidence: Four telescopes at observatories in New Mexico, France, Italy and Germany fire lasers at them

facts.claim: Distance precision
facts.evidence: within a fraction of an inch (a few millimeters)

facts.claim: Average Earth-Moon distance (NASA article)
facts.evidence: average distance of 239,000 miles (385,000 kilometers)

facts.claim: Moon recedes from Earth
facts.evidence: increases by 1.5 inches (3.8 centimeters) a year

facts.claim: Tidal cause of the recession
facts.evidence: causes the Moon to spiral away from Earth by 0.1 inches (3 millimeters) each month

facts.claim: Moon flexes up and down each month
facts.evidence: vary as much as six inches (15 centimeters) up and down each month

facts.claim: Lunar laser ranging shows the Moon has a fluid core
facts.evidence: shows that the Moon has a fluid core

facts.claim: Test of Einstein: no composition-dependent difference in gravity
facts.evidence: finds no difference in how gravity attracts the Moon and Earth due to their makeup

facts.claim: Lunar orbit and orientation needed by orbiters and landers
facts.evidence: The lunar orbit and the orientation of the rotating Moon are needed by spacecraft that orbit and land on the Moon.

facts.claim: NASA approved a new generation of lunar reflectors
facts.evidence: NASA has approved a new generation of reflectors

facts.claim: Research with Apollo-era reflectors continues
facts.evidence: Research with these Apollo-era lunar retroreflectors continues to this day.

status.label: Left in place since 21 July 1969 · nothing on it operates
status.detail: Only the descent stage remains at Tranquility Base. The ascent stage carried the crew back to lunar orbit and was later released. NASA's catalog says its fate is unknown and assumes it crashed into the Moon within a few months.

location.site: Tranquility Base, Mare Tranquillitatis (Sea of Tranquility)
location.convention: Measured from Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter images (mean Earth/polar axis frame)

timeline.text: The descent engine begins a 756-second burn toward the surface.
Eagle lands in the Sea of Tranquility.
Armstrong steps off the ladder onto the Moon.
The ascent stage lifts off. The descent stage stays behind as its launch pad.
The site's position is measured from Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter images.

status.label: Still used by observatories today · needs no power
status.detail: The array has no electronics. Telescopes on Earth fire laser pulses at the Apollo arrays and time the echoes. NASA's 2019 article names four observatories, in New Mexico, France, Italy and Germany.

location.site: Tranquility Base, about 5 m north-northwest of the Apollo 11 seismometer
location.convention: Coordinates are for the experiments package site (about 17 m south of the lunar module); the reflector stood about 5 m away from it

timeline.text: Aldrin carries the reflector and the seismometer out from Eagle and sets them up.
The solar-powered seismometer stops accepting commands. The reflector, needing no power, carries on.
Apollo 14 and Apollo 15 crews leave more reflector arrays.
NASA reports the arrays are still returning data, 50 years on.
Lunar laser ranging research with Apollo-era reflectors continues.

status.label: Silent since 22 March 2010 · mission ended 25 May 2011
status.detail: Spirit got stuck in soft soil at a spot called Troy on 1 May 2009 and became a stationary science platform. After 22 March 2010 the team could not regain contact. NASA ended recovery attempts on 25 May 2011; the most likely cause was cold that made its survival heaters ineffective.

location.site: Gusev Crater. Landing site: Columbia Memorial Station. Final spot: Troy, beside Home Plate in the Columbia Hills
location.convention: Marker shows the published landing coordinates (planetocentric, east-positive). Spirit's final spot, Troy, is in the Columbia Hills, which lie about 3 km from the landing site.

timeline.text: Spirit's airbag-wrapped lander bounces 28 times, then rolls to a stop inside Gusev Crater.
First time any spacecraft grinds into a rock on Mars (a rock called Adirondack).
Reaches the summit of Husband Hill and takes 360° panoramas.
A front wheel stops turning; Spirit finds signs of an ancient explosion at Home Plate.
The dragging wheel uncovers soil that is about 90% silica.
Gets stuck in soft soil at Troy.
Last contact with Earth.
NASA ends recovery attempts and declares the mission complete.

status.label: Silent since 15 December 2022 · mission declared over
status.detail: Dust slowly covered InSight's solar panels and reduced its power. NASA declared the mission over on 21 December 2022 after two missed communication attempts; the last contact was on 15 December. NASA said it would keep listening, just in case.

location.site: Western Elysium Planitia, near Mars' equator
location.convention: NASA gives the landing site as centered at about 4.5° N, 135.9° E (planetocentric, east-positive). The marker is placed there.

timeline.text: Launches from California on an Atlas V rocket.
Lands on the flat plain of Elysium Planitia.
The arm sets the seismometer on the ground, a first on another planet.
The domed wind and thermal shield covers the seismometer.
The heat probe's "mole" tries to dig, but stops just below the surface.
Marsquake data reveal the crust, mantle and molten core.
Takes its final, very dusty selfie.
Last contact. NASA declares the mission over on 21 December.
